judgments.note: Seven domains: mental health, democracy, information/public health, cohesion, activism, business/education, privacy
Each domain gets explicit positives and negatives
Several named studies (2.73M posts, 2000 Americans, Germany hate crimes) but many claims uncited
Mechanisms per domain: algorithmic amplification, gatekeeping removal, attention-rewarding distribution, profiling
Final two sentences weigh domains and deliver definitive judgment
Compares to older media and traditional journalism's gatekeeping
No non-Western platforms named (no Douyin, VK, etc.)
Misinformation proliferation and degraded deliberative conditions discussed as ongoing trends
No policy/regulatory responses (no Section 230, COPPA, etc.)
Per-domain balance verdicts explicitly integrated in final weighing
Only Facebook named; no coverage of 3+ platform formats
Implicit purposeful-use-vs-systemic-harm weighing principle; no explicit justified methodology
No specification/justification of geographic regions analyzed
No short-term vs long-term distinction
Activism cases present but never framed as unintentional from platforms' view
Misinformation/propaganda present but not framed as foreseeable-unmitigated
No regulatory environments discussed
No counterfactual baseline defined
No platform bans/shutdowns/absence effects
Young people, minors, refugees mentioned incidentally; no systematic demographic contrasts
Academic studies, case studies, activist/journalistic reporting all used
Consistent per-domain balance framework applied throughout
No time period specified or justified
Key demographic groups not specified as analysis scope
Mental-health claims hedged with explicit causal caution; penalty not triggered
Smartphones never mentioned
No EU vs US data-protection comparison
Retweeting/likes discussed (out-group sharing, likes-not-action) but not both positive and negative feedback impacts
